gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a measured runtime at a heater-sized load. Every rival's 34–36 minutes comes from an assumed 85% efficiency. Two reviewers measured it: The Solar Lab ran the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 at 1,479 W for 37.5 min (about 924 Wh), and The Technology Man ran the Anker SOLIX C1000 Gen 2 on a 1 kW electric heater for just over 54 min (907 Wh). From those and other measured capacities, each ~1 kWh candidate gives about 36–38 min on high.
standout_why: I compared against four rival pages. Volt & Valley (cited) uses Wh × 0.85 for every model, e.g. Jackery 1000 v2 about 36 min and AC180 about 39 min, with no measured data and no cost per runtime. Lights On Lab (cited) says its chart is 'Calculated, not measured'. UTrendCo (cited) says 'Runtime figures are our calculations, not lab results' and calls the Jackery 1000 v2 on high 'at the limit, not advised', with no test behind that. Tested Watts (cited, rank 1) returned a certificate error and I could not read it, so I have not checked it. None of the pages I read gives a reviewer-measured Wh or minutes at a heater-level load, or a price per minute of heat. Their minute counts land close to the measured ones, so the new part is the evidence and the per-product spread, not a different headline number.
decides: The measurements confirm the headline answer of about half an hour (36–38 min measured or derived, against the 34–35 min rivals assume). They also weaken the 'at its limit; not recommended' cell our page gives the Jackery 1000 v2: The Solar Lab held 1,479 W for 37.5 min and 1,500–1,560 W for 10 min without a trip. For value, the BLUETTI AC180 at $499 is the cheapest candidate per minute of heat that I could price: about $13 per minute against about $16 for the EcoFlow DELTA 3. There is also a caution for the C1000 Gen 2: The Technology Man's UK unit overheated after 26 min on a 2 kW heater, so it can't be assumed to run safely right at the inverter limit.
